items.answer:

items.question: What does a study contain in addition to the domains based on the general observation classes?
items.answer:
In addition to the 3 general observation classes, a study will generally include a set of other special-purpose datasets ([1], [3]).

More specifically, the SDTM includes 4 types of datasets other than those based on the general observation classes ([5]):

- **Domain datasets with subject-level data that do not conform to 1 of the 3 general observation classes**: Demographics (DM), Comments (CO), Subject Elements (SE), and Subject Visits (SV), described in Section 5, Models for Special-purpose Domains ([5]).
- **Trial Design Model (TDM) datasets**, which represent information about the study design but do not contain subject data, such as Trial Arms (TA) and Trial Elements (TE), described in Section 7, Trial Design Model Datasets ([5]).
- **Relationship datasets**, such as the RELREC and SUPP-- datasets, described in Section 8, Representing Relationships and Data ([5]).
- **Study Reference datasets**, including Device Identifiers (DI) and Non-host Organism Identifiers (OI), which provide structures for representing study-specific terminology used in subject data, described in Section 9, Study References ([5]).

items.question: Are sponsors allowed to split one domain into several physical datasets?
items.answer:
Yes. Sponsors may choose to split a domain of topically related information into physically separate datasets [1].

Key points from the documentation:

- **General observation class domains** may be split according to values in --CAT; when split on --CAT, --CAT must not be null [1].
- **The Findings About (FA) domain** may alternatively be split based on the domain of the value in --OBJ (e.g., FACM stores findings about CM records) [1]. FA data may be represented in a single FA dataset (potentially split per Section 4.1.6), or as separate datasets with unique custom 2-character domain codes [2].
- **Rules when splitting** (to ensure datasets can be appended back into one domain dataset) [1]:
  1. DOMAIN must be consistent across the separate datasets (e.g., QS, FA).
  2. All variables requiring a domain prefix (e.g., --TESTCD, --LOC) must use the DOMAIN value as the prefix.
  3. --SEQ must be unique within USUBJID across all split datasets.
  4. For relationship datasets (SUPPxx, FAxx, CO, RELREC) relating back to split parent domains, IDVAR would generally be --SEQ; if another variable is used (e.g., --GRPID, --REFID, --SPID), care must be taken that parent records across split datasets have unique values for that IDVAR.
  5. Permissible variables included in one split dataset need not be included in all split datasets.
  6. For 2-letter domain codes (other than SUPPxx and RELREC), split dataset names can be up to 4 characters (domain name plus up to 2 additional characters, e.g., QS36; FACM for FA split by parent domain).
  7. Supplemental Qualifier datasets for split domains are also split (e.g., SUPPQS36, SUPPFACM), with RDOMAIN containing the 2-character domain code (e.g., QS, FA).
  8. In RELREC, for a dataset-level relationship with a split FA domain, RDOMAIN may contain the 4-character dataset name rather than "FA".
  9. Naming of split AP datasets is addressed in the SDTMIG: Associated Persons.
  10. Metadata representation is addressed in the Define-XML specification and the MSG for SDTMIG.

- **Regulatory caveat:** submission of split SDTM domains may be subject to additional dataset-splitting conventions defined by regulators via technical specifications and/or as negotiated with regulatory reviewers [1].

Note: Excerpt 2 references "Section 4.1.6, Additional Guidance on Dataset Naming" for splitting FA data, while the detailed splitting rules appear in Section 4.1.7 [1][2].

items.question: Which variables group records within a domain, and who assigns their values?
items.answer:
# Grouping Variables in SDTM Domains and Assignment of Their Values

## Variables that group records

The SDTMIG identifies the following grouping variables, presented in a hierarchy [3]:

- **STUDYID** — groups all records describing that study (across subjects) [3]
- **DOMAIN** — groups all records describing that domain (across subjects) [3]
- **--CAT (Category)** and **--SCAT (Subcategory)** — further subset groups within the domain; generally meaningful within a particular domain, though the same values may be used across related domains (e.g., MH and AE) provided the meanings are the same [3]
- **USUBJID** — groups all records describing that subject [3]
- **--GRPID** — further groups (subsets) records within USUBJID; all records in the same domain with the same --GRPID value are a group of records within USUBJID [1][3]
- **--LNKID** and **--LNKGRP** — grouping identifiers used to link records in separate domains (one-to-many and many-to-one relationships, respectively) [1]

Additionally, although **--SPID** and **--REFID** are Identifier variables, they may sometimes be used as grouping variables and may also have meaning across domains [1][3].

Domain-specific examples: **REGRPID** ("Optional group identifier, used to link together a block of related records within a subject in a domain") [5] and **PPGRPID** ("Used to tie together a block of related records in a single domain to support relationships within the domain and between domains") [6].

## Who assigns the values

- **--CAT/--SCAT**: generally defined by the sponsor or used by the investigator at the point of collection, not after assessing the value of Findings results [1]. They are known (identified) about the data before it is collected and may have controlled terminology [1].
- **--GRPID**: usually assigned during or after data collection **at the discretion of the sponsor**; values are sponsor-defined and not subject to controlled terminology [1]. The values can be any values the sponsor chooses; if values with embedded meaning are used (rather than arbitrary numbers), they should be consistent across the submission [2]. --GRPID has no inherent meaning across subjects or across domains [2].
- **--REFID**: values are sponsor-defined and can be any alphanumeric strings the sponsor chooses, consistent with their internal practices [2].
- **--RESCAT** (Findings domains): can be used to categorize results **after the fact** [1].

## Key distinctions

The primary distinctions between --CAT/--SCAT and --GRPID are [1]:
1. --CAT/--SCAT are known (identified) about the data before it is collected.
2. --CAT/--SCAT values group data across subjects.
3. --CAT/--SCAT may have some controlled terminology.
4. --GRPID is usually assigned during or after data collection at the discretion of the sponsor.
5. --GRPID groups data only within a subject.
6. --GRPID values are sponsor-defined and will not be subject to controlled terminology.

Consequently, data that would be the same across subjects is usually more appropriate in --CAT/--SCAT, while data that would vary across subjects is usually more appropriate in --GRPID [1].

judge.rationale: All factual claims in the answer are directly supported by the excerpts: the grouping variables (STUDYID, DOMAIN, --CAT/--SCAT, USUBJID, --GRPID, --LNKID/--LNKGRP, --SPID/--REFID) and their assignment (sponsor/investigator for --CAT/--SCAT, sponsor discretion during/after collection for --GRPID, sponsor-defined for --REFID, after-the-fact for --RESCAT) all appear in the cited excerpts. Citation markers correctly map to supporting excerpts ([1] and [3] for section 4.2.6, [2] for section 8.1, [5]/[6] for the variable rows). The answer agrees with and extends the reference answer accurately.

items.question: How is controlled terminology represented in a domain specification?
items.answer:
Controlled terminology is represented in a domain specification's "Controlled Terms, Codelist or Format" column in the following ways (as of SDTMIG v3.3) [1][4][6]:

- A single asterisk (*) when CDISC Controlled Terminology is not currently available but the SDS Team expects sponsors may have their own controlled terminology and/or CDISC may develop it in the future [1][4][6].
- The single applicable value for the variable DOMAIN (e.g., "PR") [1][4][6].
- The name of a CDISC codelist, represented as a hyperlink in parentheses (e.g., "(NY)") [1][4][6].
- A short reference to an external terminology (e.g., "MedDRA", "ISO 3166-1 alpha-3") [1][4][6].

In addition, the column is used to indicate variables that use an ISO 8601 format [1][4][6].

Related points:
- Terms from controlled terminology should use the case that appears in the source codelist or code system (e.g., CDISC codelist or external code system such as MedDRA) [4][6].
- The controlled terminology or a reference to it should be included in the Define-XML document wherever applicable, with all values in the study's permissible value set included whether or not they appear in submitted data; null values should not be included in the permissible value set [6].
- When a domain or dataset specification includes a codelist for a variable, only values that were part of planned data collection should be included in the Define-XML document (e.g., --PRESP is associated with the NY codelist but only "Y" is allowed) [2][3][6].
- Controlled terminology or human-readable text should be used instead of arbitrary number codes; numeric code values may be submitted as Supplemental Qualifiers if necessary [2][3].
- The sponsor is expected to provide the dictionary name and version used to map terms via Define-XML external codelist attributes [3].

Example from the FA domain specification: FATESTCD is shown as "Char (FATESTCD)" and FAORRESU as "Char (UNIT)", while FACAT and FASCAT are shown as "Char *" [5].

The four representation methods (asterisk, DOMAIN value, codelist hyperlink in parentheses, external terminology reference) plus ISO 8601 format are stated in Excerpts 1, 4, and 6. The related points on text case (Excerpts 4, 6), Define-XML permissible values and null exclusion (Excerpt 6), planned data collection subset (Excerpts 2, 3, 6), avoiding arbitrary number codes (Excerpts 2, 3), and dictionary name/version via external codelist attributes (Excerpt 3) are all supported. The FA example (FATESTCD as Char (FATESTCD), FAORRESU as Char (UNIT), FACAT/FASCAT as Char *) is supported by Excerpt 5. Citations are accurately attached to the supporting excerpts. items.question: How is the precision of a date or time represented?
items.answer:
Precision of a date or time is represented through the ISO 8601 standard: precision (also called "completeness" or "representations with reduced accuracy") is inferred from the presence or absence of components in the date and/or time values [1]. Missing components are represented by right truncation or by a hyphen for intermediate components that are missing [1]. If date and time values are completely missing, the SDTM date field should be null [1]. Every component except year is represented as 2 digits; years are 4 digits, and 1-digit numbers for other components are padded with a leading zero [1][2].

Examples of right truncation [2]:
- Date/time to the nearest second: 2003-12-15T13:14:17
- Unknown seconds: 2003-12-15T13:14
- Unknown minutes and seconds: 2003-12-15T13
- Unknown time: 2003-12-15
- Unknown day and time: 2003-12
- Unknown month, day, and time: 2003

If no time component is represented, the [T] time designator must be omitted [1][2]. Fractional seconds may be represented (e.g., 2003-12-15T13:14:17.123) [2].

For missing intermediate components, a single hyphen indicates the omitted component while expected delimiters are kept in place (e.g., unknown hour with known minutes: 2003-12-15T-:15) [6].

Intervals of uncertainty are represented by concatenating the most complete known start and end date/time values, separated by a solidus (e.g., 2003-12-15T10:00/2003-12-15T10:30; 2003-12-01/2003-12-10; 2003-01-01/2003-06-30) [4][5][6].

items.question: Do all time points require the same set of variables to be identified uniquely?
items.answer:

- The set of time-point variables used varies by trial. In some trials only one value of `--TPTREF` (e.g., "DOSE") is needed and it "would be populated, but would not contribute to uniqueness" [1].

items.question: What approach does the guide use to represent a group of tests that were not done?
items.answer:
The guide offers two sponsor options for representing tests not done: (1) submit individual records for each test not done, or (2) submit 1 record for a group of tests that were not done [3].

For the single-record approach representing a group of tests not done, the guide specifies [1][3]:

- `--TESTCD` should be `--ALL`
- `--TEST` should be `<Domain description>`
- `--CAT` should be `<Name of group of tests>`
- `--ORRES` should be null
- `--STAT` should be "NOT DONE"
- `--REASND`, if collected, might be "Specimen lost"

Example given for urinalysis tests not done [1][3]:
- LBTESTCD = "LBALL"
- LBTEST = "Laboratory Test Results"
- LBCAT = "URINALYSIS"
- LBORRES = null
- LBSTAT = "NOT DONE"
- LBREASND, if collected, might be "Subject could not void"

The examples also illustrate this pattern across domains: LBTESTCD = "LBALL" with LBSTAT = "NOT DONE" for a hematology category not done at a visit, and with a null LBCAT when none of the LB tests were done [1]; EGTESTCD = "EGALL" and EGSTAT = "NOT DONE" when there were no ECG results [1][2]; and VSTESTCD = "VSALL" and VSSTAT = "NOT DONE" when there were no Vital Signs results [2][5].

items.question: How does a result of NORMAL or ABNORMAL relate to clinical significance?
items.answer:
Results of "NORMAL"/"ABNORMAL" are distinct from clinical significance; they are not equivalent and are represented by different variables.

- Clinical significance is captured in the --CLSIG (Clinically Significant) variable, defined as "an indication as to whether an observation is clinically significant based on judgment," with examples "Y", "N" [3]. It is used for collected assessments of clinical significance of a result [3].
- "Separate from clinical significance are results of 'NORMAL' or 'ABNORMAL', or lab values that are out of normal range" [2].
- For an ECG test with EGTESTCD = "INTP" (addressing the ECG as a whole), the result should be "NORMAL" or "ABNORMAL"; the same record may also carry EGCLSIG indicating whether the result is clinically significant [2]. Similarly, a vital signs or lab record with a measurement may have a normal range and normal range indicator, and could also have --CLSIG indicating clinical significance [2].
- Example: EGCLSIG = "Y" indicates that an ECG result of "ATRIAL FIBRILLATION" was clinically significant [2].
- In the NV domain example, individual VEP components are interpreted as normal/abnormal via NVNRIND, and the overall interpretation (NVTESTCD = "INTP") is represented in NVORRES as "ABNORMAL"; clinical significance is not shown in that example [4].
- For vital signs, clinical significance is represented in VSCLSIG, per Section 4.5.5 [5].

In short: NORMAL/ABNORMAL (or normal-range indicators) describe the interpretation of a result relative to normality, whereas --CLSIG separately records whether that result was judged clinically significant [2][3].

items.question: Which identifier is used when a comment refers to a specific domain record?
items.answer:
The identifier used is **IDVAR** in the CO (Comments) domain, which holds the name of the identifying variable in the parent dataset that identifies the record(s) to which the comment applies (e.g., AESEQ or CMGRPID) [1][2]. It is used only when individual comments are related to domain records, and is null for comments collected on separate CRFs [1][2].

The corresponding value is carried in **IDVARVAL** (Identifying Variable Value), which holds the value of the identifying variable of the parent record(s), again used only when individual comments are related to domain records [3].

Grouping variables can also be used as the value in IDVAR to identify comments with relationships to multiple domain records (e.g., a comment applying to a group of concomitant medications taken as combination therapy); however, a single comment may only relate to a group of records in one domain, since RDOMAIN can have only one value [4][5].

items.question: What does the subject visits dataset record?
items.answer:
The SV (Subject Visits) dataset is a special-purpose domain that "contains information for each subject's actual and planned visits" [6]. Its structure is "One record per actual or planned visit per subject" [1][3][6].

Key points on what it records:

- **Purpose/consolidation:** It "consolidates information about the timing of subject visits that is otherwise spread over domains that include the visit variables (VISITNUM and possibly VISIT and/or VISITDY)" [6]. Unless the beginning and end of each visit is collected, populating SV involves derivations [6].
- **Start/end timing:** SVSTDTC and SVENDTC capture the start and end date/time of the visit; where only a single date exists per visit, both are populated with that single date, and for multiday visits they reflect the actual span [6][5].
- **Planned vs. unplanned:** SVPRESP indicates whether the visit was planned (value "Y" for planned visits, null for unplanned) [6]. SVOCCUR records whether a planned visit occurred (null for unplanned visits) [6]. SVOCCUR = "N" records are only created for planned visits expected to occur before the end of the subject's participation [2].
- **Reason and mode:** SVREASOC gives the reason for the SVOCCUR value (e.g., why a visit did not occur) [6]; SVCNTMOD records how the visit was conducted (e.g., "IN PERSON", "TELEPHONE CALL", "IVRS") [6][5].
- **Study days:** VISITDY is the planned study day (not populated for unplanned visits) [5][6]; SVSTDY and SVENDY are the actual study days corresponding to SVSTDTC and SVENDTC [5].
- **Use:** The SV dataset "provides reviewers with a summary of a subject's visits over the course of their participation in a study," and comparison with the TV dataset supports identification of planned but not expected visits and departures from planned timing [6].

Note: Excerpt 4 (FA domain) is not relevant to SV.

items.question: Which domains are grouped as specimen-based findings domains?
items.answer:
The specimen-based findings domains are grouped in Section 6.3.5, which covers domains representing laboratory measurements, tests, or examinations performed on collected biological specimens (e.g., blood, urine, tumor tissue) [1][2].

The domains explicitly named in the excerpts as belonging to this group are:

- **IS** (Immunogenicity Specimen Assessments) [1][2][3]
- **LB** (Laboratory Test Results) [1][2][5]
- **MB/MS** (Microbiology) [1][2]

items.question: What does the pharmacokinetics parameters domain contain?
items.answer:
The PP domain is a findings domain that contains pharmacokinetic parameters derived from pharmacokinetic concentration-time (PC) data [2]. It is structured as one record per PK parameter per time-concentration profile per modeling method per subject [2].

Key content characteristics:

- **Derived dataset**: PP is a derived dataset and may be produced from an analysis dataset with a different structure; some sponsors may need to normalize their analysis dataset to fit the SDTM-based PP domain [1].
- **Parameter identification**: PPTESTCD holds the short name of the PK parameter (e.g., "AUCALL", "TMAX", "CMAX") and PPTEST holds the parameter name (e.g., "AUC All", "Time of CMAX", "Max Conc") [2]. PPCAT should be the name of the analyte in PCTEST whose profile the parameter is associated with [2]. PPSCAT categorizes the model type used to calculate the PK parameters (e.g., "COMPARTMENTAL", "NON-COMPARTMENTAL") [2].
- **Results**: PPORRES/PPORRESU hold the result and original units; PPSTRESC/PPSTRESN/PPSTRESU hold the standardized result and units [2]. Separate codelists are used for PPORRESU/PPSTRESU depending on whether the parameter is normalized: "PKUNIT" for non-normalized parameters; "PKUDMG" and "PKUDUG" when normalized by dose amount in milligrams or micrograms; "PKUWG" and "PKUWKG" when normalized by weight in grams or kilograms [1].
- **Not-calculated parameters**: PPSTAT indicates a parameter was not calculated (should be null if a result exists in PPORRES), and PPREASND describes why (e.g., "INSUFFICIENT DATA") [2].
- **Additional information**: Information pertaining to all parameters (e.g., number of exponents, model weighting) should be submitted in the SUPPPP dataset [1]. Any Identifiers, Timing variables, or Findings general observation class qualifiers may be added to PP, but --BODSYS and --SEV would not generally be used [1].

Examples in the documentation show parameters such as TMAX, CMAX, AUCALL, LAMZHL, VZO, CLO, AUCINT, RAAUC, AUCIFO, and AUCIFP for parent drug and metabolites in plasma and urine [1][3][6].

items.question: How are dataset names derived from the domain code?
items.answer:
**Standard rule**

Each study subject domain dataset is distinguished by a unique 2-character code, stored in the DOMAIN variable; this code is used in the dataset name, as the value of DOMAIN in that dataset, and as a prefix for most variable names in that dataset [1]. SDTM datasets are normally named to be consistent with the domain code; for example, the Demographics dataset (DM) is named dm.xpt [2]. Standard domain codes are listed in the SDTM Domain Abbreviation codelist, C66734, in CDISC Controlled Terminology [2].

**Exceptions**

Exceptions to the naming rule are described in Section 4.1.7, Splitting Domains, for general observation class datasets, and in Section 8, Representing Relationships and Data, for RELREC and SUPP-- datasets [2].

**Split datasets**

For domains with 2-letter domain codes (i.e., other than SUPPxx and RELREC), split dataset names can be up to 4 characters in length. For example, if splitting by --CAT, dataset names would be the domain name plus up to 2 additional characters (e.g., QS36 for SF-36). If splitting Findings About by parent domain, the dataset name would be the domain code "FA" plus the 2-character domain code for the parent domain (e.g., "FACM") [4]. Supplemental Qualifier datasets for split domains are also split, with nomenclature including the additional 1 to 2 characters used to identify the split dataset (e.g., SUPPQS36, SUPPFACM); the value of RDOMAIN in the SUPP-- datasets remains the 2-character domain code (e.g., QS, FA) [4].

**Custom domains**

Domain codes beginning with the letters X, Y, and Z have been reserved for the creation of custom domains, with any letter or number permitted in the second position; use of codes beginning with X, Y, or Z is optional and not required for custom domains [2][4].

items.question: How are clinical encounters and visits represented in the submitted data?
items.answer:
Based on the provided excerpts, clinical encounters and visits are represented as follows:

**Definition and concept**
- Visits are defined as "clinical encounters" and are described using the timing variables VISIT, VISITNUM, and VISITDY [4]. A clinical encounter derives from trials with outpatients where subjects interact with the investigator during visits to the clinical site, but the term is also used where a trial visit may not correspond to a physical visit (e.g., inpatient time subdivided into visits); the protocol should specify what contacts are considered visits and how they are defined [1].

**Planned visits (Trial Design — TV)**
- The Trial Visits (TV) dataset contains the planned order and number of visits in the study within each arm, describing the allowable/planned values for VISIT, VISITNUM, and VISITDY (subsequently used as timing variables for collected study data) and rules for starting and ending each visit [3][4].
- TV structure is "One record per planned Visit per Arm"; for blinded trials where the schedule is the same for all arms, ARMCD should be left blank [4].

items.question: What additional conventions may apply when a domain is split into several datasets?
items.answer:
The provided documentation identifies the following additional conventions that may apply when a domain is split into several datasets:

**Regulator-defined conventions**
- Submission of split SDTM domains may be subject to additional dataset-splitting conventions as defined by regulators via technical specifications and/or as negotiated with regulatory reviewers [1][2].

**Metadata and naming references**
- The SDTM Define-XML specification should be consulted for details regarding metadata representation when a domain is split into different datasets; additional examples are in the Metadata Submission Guideline (MSG) for SDTMIG [1][2].
- For the naming of split Associated Persons (AP) datasets, see the SDTM Implementation Guide: Associated Persons [1][2].

**Findings About (FA) split conventions**
- When splitting FA by parent domain, the dataset name is "FA" plus the 2-character parent domain code (e.g., FACE, FAMH); this naming convention may be used even when the study has only 1 FA dataset that is not being split [3].
- Supplemental qualifier datasets are managed at the split-file level (e.g., suppface.xpt, suppfamh.xpt), with RDOMAIN = "FA" within each [3].
- If a dataset-level RELREC is defined (e.g., between CE and FACE), RDOMAIN may contain up to 4 characters to describe the relationship between parent and child records [3].

**Supplemental qualifiers for split domains**
- Supplemental Qualifier datasets for split domains are also split, with nomenclature including the additional 1 to 2 characters used to identify the split dataset (e.g., SUPPQS36, SUPPFACM); RDOMAIN in the SUPP-- datasets remains the 2-character domain code (e.g., QS, FA) [2].
- When split data require longer names such as SUPPFAMH, and a name with the SUPP fragment would be too long (e.g., SUPPAPFAMH), the "SUPP" portion should be shortened to "SQ" (e.g., SQAPFAMH) [6].

**RELREC for split FA domains**
- In RELREC, if a dataset-level relationship is defined for a split Findings About domain, RDOMAIN may contain the 4-character dataset name rather than the domain name "FA" [2].
